sources.news_title: Virginia senator’s case is two different stories, depending on who’s telling it
sources.text:
Depending on who is telling the story, Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas is either the head of a $4.5 million criminal weed enterprise or the latest critic of President Donald Trump to be charged by his Justice Department — in her case, just 12 days before an election.
On Thursday, federal prosecutors unsealed an indictment charging Lucas with racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to distribute marijuana, among other offenses. Authorities also charged six others, including two of Lucas’ daughters and her grandson. The charges against Lucas, the Democratic president pro tempore of Virginia’s state Senate who was instrumental in an ultimately unsuccessful redistricting push, come nearly six months after the FBI raided her office and a nearby cannabis shop she co-owns in Portsmouth, Virginia.
Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.™
Point phone camera here
For decades, the Justice Department has generally avoided public action against political figures in the final weeks before an election, a practice known as the 60-day rule. Attorney General Todd Blanche said there was nothing improper about the timing, noting Lucas isn’t on the ballot this year. One of her co-defendants is, however: her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke is running for Portsmouth City Council.
The case also comes 10 days after federal agents searched the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., as part of an immigration fraud investigation. Omar, who is seeking a fifth term in the House, has not been charged with any crimes. She is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, who suggested this week that Omar might be deported or imprisoned, calling her native Somalia a “s— house.”
According to sources who spoke to CBS News, Blanche was aware of the search, and the department consulted its Public Integrity Section, which handles politically sensitive cases. The Trump administration has cut that section from between 35 and 40 lawyers to about two.
The dual narratives
The split-screen media narrative about the Lucas case started with the May search. Fox News, seen as friendly to the Trump administration, was the first outlet to report the search, according to the Virginia Mercury, and a Fox correspondent reported live from outside Lucas’s office as it unfolded.
No one has confirmed Fox was tipped off. But Virginia House Speaker Don Scott, a Democrat, questioned in a statement that day whether the network knew about the raid in advance. It echoed 2019, when then-Fox host Tucker Carlson asked how CNN cameras arrived at Trump ally Roger Stone’s home before the FBI did. Stone was later charged with lying to authorities investigating Russia’s alleged interference in the 2016 election, but Trump pardoned him before leaving office in 2021.
Coverage of Thursday’s charges broke along the same lines. Fox News emphasized the Justice Department’s description of a family-run “Lucas Enterprise,” while NBC News highlighted the timing, calling the move unusual so close to an election. Lucas herself framed it as the federal government’s “full weight” brought against “an 82-year-old great-grandmother.”
What the indictment alleges
Prosecutors allege that since at least 2019, Lucas led a family-run operation that sold illegal marijuana through The Cannabis Outlet, a Portsmouth shop she co-owns. They say she used her clout in Richmond to shape marijuana laws in her favor and shield the business from state scrutiny. Virginia allows adults to possess marijuana, but recreational sales remain illegal until 2027.
According to the indictment, Lucas arranged for the purchase and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana — about the same weight as a typical front-loading washing machine — and oversaw laundering of the proceeds. Prosecutors also allege she paid $750,000 for a shell company created to help a co-conspirator obtain a state marijuana license, then received what prosecutors called a “bribery payment” in return.
The 45-page indictment cites an FBI wiretap of Lucas’ cellphone in March and April. In one call, she allegedly told an unindicted co-conspirator that a recreational cannabis license was her family’s path to “generational wealth.”
State regulators cited The Cannabis Outlet, which sold hemp and CBD products, in 2023 and 2024 for selling cannabis products that didn’t comply with state law, according to the indictment. When agents searched it and a second store, The CBD Shoppe, in May, prosecutors say they found marijuana and guns at both.
The investigation began under the Biden administration, and Blanche rejected claims of political motive. “We don’t do political paybacks,” he said.
Lucas’ case joins a string of prosecutions of Trump critics that have drawn accusations of retribution. The Justice Department indicted former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James in 2025. But a judge later dismissed both cases after ruling the prosecutor who brought them had been unlawfully appointed. The department is appealing, and it indicted Comey again this year. Former national security adviser John Bolton, whose investigation also began under Biden, pleaded guilty in June to illegally retaining classified documents.
The timing
The 60-day rule isn’t written policy. The Justice Manual only bars prosecutors from timing a case “for the purpose” of affecting an election, which is the standard Blanche invoked Thursday. But the practice took hold after the Watergate scandal, when politicized prosecutions cost the department public trust, according to Thomas Hogan, a former federal prosecutor who teaches at South Texas College of Law Houston.
A grand jury indicted Lucas last week, and Hogan said nothing stopped the department from waiting. “Normally you would just wait until the midterms were over to announce this indictment,” he said.
Other former prosecutors said the Omar search broke with that practice. Randall Eliason, a George Washington University law professor and former public corruption prosecutor, told Al Jazeera that it appeared to depart from past practice, though nothing enforces the policy. Mary McCord, a former senior Justice Department official, called it a departure from “long-standing internal guidance” in an interview with The Hill.
Others argue the norm was never binding. Abhishek Kambli, a senior Justice Department official in the Trump administration, told Fox News that a 60-day requirement isn’t in the department’s manual.
What’s next
Democrats have cast Lucas’ case as payback for her role in an attempt to redraw Virginia’s congressional districts to heavily favor candidates from her party. In April, voters approved the map, which would have added four Democratic-leaning House seats, but the Virginia Supreme Court threw it out and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to revive it.
Authorities released Lucas on her own recognizance after a brief court appearance Thursday, when prosecutors didn’t seek to detain her. She remains Senate president pro tem and chair of the committee that writes Virginia’s budget, and she isn’t up for reelection until 2027. Her daughter, though, will be on Portsmouth ballots in less than two weeks.
However the case ends, the timing adds to questions about the department’s independence. Gregg Nunziata, a former DOJ lawyer who leads the Society for the Rule of Law, told Roll Call that after the Omar search that politicians should be prosecuted when the facts support it but “the public has to have confidence in those actions.”

Top Virginia Democrat, Family Members Indicted in Marijuana Conspiracy
A federal grand jury has indicted the top Democrat in Virginia’s Senate and some of her family members for running an illegal marijuana trafficking operation that involved wire fraud and money laundering.
Louise Lucas, president pro tempore of the Senate, and six defendants, including her daughters and a grandson, face an eight-count indictment, including a firearms charge.
In 2022, the Virginia Mercury reported that one of Lucas’ stores sold an illegal product.
Lucas was proud of her business, and a month before that story was published had bragged about being a “grandma” marijuana peddler.
She played the race card today on X.
The Charges
The longtime Democrat, the indictment says, is the queenpin of a “criminal enterprise” that included “a close-knit group of associates and family members, including her two daughters and her grandson,” the Justice Department reported:
Lucas allegedly approved and directed activities of the enterprise, including arranging for the acquisition and distribution of 100 kilograms or more of marijuana and supervising the laundering of marijuana proceeds.
Lucas also exploited her “political position to insulate the Lucas Enterprise from criminal scrutiny and to influence legislation benefiting the enterprise,” DOJ continued:
Carlton Upton Jr., 54, of Chesapeake, Virginia, was Lucas’ business partner in VA Freedom Life, an umbrella for The CBD Shoppe and The Cannabis Outlet beginning in 2019. Upton also managed the CBD Shoppe and allegedly worked with Lucas to obtain a recreational marijuana license to benefit the Lucas Enterprise. In April 2020, Upton allegedly made materially false attestations on an application for an Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) for Virginia Freedom Life, which was funded in the amount of $11,800.
In 2021, Lucas and her daughter, Lisa Lucas-Burke, opened The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth, Virginia. Another daughter of Lucas, Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and Lucas-Lamb’s son, Ryan Eichelberger, allegedly acquired marijuana and supervised its distribution and managed The Cannabis Outlet for the Lucas Enterprise. On Feb. 1, 2022, Lucas listed herself as President and CEO of VA Freedom Life on the Virginia Conflict of Interest and Ethics Advisory General Assembly Statement of Economic Interests form.
Lucas also bought “a shell holding company for a co-conspirator’s expected Virginia recreational marijuana license” for $750,000, the indictment charges.
When FBI agents raided the two stores, they found firearms.
As the Virginia Mercury reported, “the case became public May 6, when federal agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and cannabis businesses.”
The eight counts are as follows:
- Count One: Racketeering conspiracy;
- Count Two: Conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana;
- Count Three: Conspiracy to launder money;
- Count Four: Conspiracy to commit honest services fraud;
- Counts Five and Six: Maintaining drug-involved premises;
- Count Seven: Possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-involved crime; and,
- Count Eight: Wire fraud.
Louise Lucas and Lisa Lucas-Burke face counts one through five. Prince Albert William Hudson III: counts one through three. Ryan Eichelberger: counts one, two, three, five, and seven. Theresa Lucas-Lamb: one, two, three, and five. Carlton Upton Jr.: one through four, six, and eight. Tameka Johnson: two, three, and six.
Kash Patel’s News Conference
“Ms. Lucas has many things to answer for on the allegation,” FBI chief Kash Patel said at a news conference:
The purpose of her enterprise included trafficking large quantities of illegal marijuana, creating generational wealth for members and associates of her criminal enterprise, recycling drug proceeds to expand the operation that she launched and created, and steering marijuana licenses to entities in which members held financial interest. During her time as a Virginia state senator, instead of enforcing the law, she was actually breaking the law as alleged in the indictment, and then using her position of power and public trust to deflect and defend against her own criminal enterprise — truly the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official.
Patel cited Lucas’ X post.
“I’m a 78 year grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannibis store,” Lucas bragged on January 24, 2022:
And I’m the last thing standing between The GOP and total control of Virginia. That’s worth an RT!
An RT is a retweet.
“Did I mention my store is on High Street in Portsmouth 😂😎?” she wrote later that day.
On X today, the black lawmaker strongly implied that the case was a racial attack.
“The full weight of the federal government [has] been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother,” Lucas said:
I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now.
I am not new to this. I’m true to this.
I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.
Website Report
The Virginia Mercury investigated Lucas’ Cannabis Outlet and found that it was retailing an illegal substance, delta-9 THC, that in concentrations of more than 0.3 percent is a Schedule 1 controlled substance; i.e., one that has a “high potential for abuse” and “no medical use.”
“The Mercury had two products analyzed — the cereal bar and a vape cartridge that claimed to be lab tested but offered no indication of what was inside,” the website reported:
[Michelle] Peace, the [Virginia Commonwealth University] forensic scientist, said both appeared to be synthetic cannabis products and while both contained delta-8 THC, both also contained quantities of delta-9 THC that would make them plainly illegal to sell in Virginia.

Virginia state senator indicted in connection with marijuana business
The Justice Department indicted Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the most powerful Democrats in the commonwealth, as part of a long-running corruption investigation involving a family-run marijuana business.
The indictment, which was returned by a federal grand jury in Virginia last week and unsealed Thursday morning, alleges that Lucas and her relatives set up a business to sell marijuana before the substance was legalized for recreational sales in the commonwealth. Lucas, who co-owns a marijuana business, has turned herself in to authorities, while multiple members of her family were arrested Thursday morning.
Federal authorities charged her with five crimes, including allegations that she participated in an illegal conspiracy of possessing marijuana with intent to distribute, conspired to money launder, maintaining a drug involved premise, and conspired to commit honest services fraud.
Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, appearing together during a news conference Thursday to announce the charges, said the case was about more than a state senator selling marijuana, portraying it instead as a racketeering case involving a powerful lawmaker using her position to enrich herself.
“During her time as Virginia state senator, instead of enforcing the law, she was actually breaking the law as alleged in the indictment and then using her position of power and public trust to deflect and defend against her own criminal enterprise,” Patel said. “Truly the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official.”
Lucas’s six alleged co-conspirators were charged with similar crimes. Her grandson was also charged with possessing a firearm in furtherance of drug trafficking.
The indictment of Lucas (D-Portsmouth), the 82-year-old president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate, is a staggering turn in the long career of the brash-talking grandmother. She has amassed considerable influence among Democrats in Virginia and frequently uses social media to taunt and lambaste Republicans, including President Donald Trump.
In a statement Thursday, she pledged to fight the charges.
“I grew up under Jim Crow,” Lucas said in a statement, referring to laws that segregated the South for decades after slavery was barred. “I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now.”
Anthony M. Capozzolo, an attorney for Lucas, said in a statement that he was “surprised and disheartened” by the charges and Lucas’s arrest, adding that the lawmaker denied all the charges.
Capozzolo also rebuked Blanche and Patel, criticizing what he called “the gratuitous, misleading statements made by the Attorney General and the Director of the FBI at the highly unusual press conference that was held.”
Lucas is not up for reelection, and Virginia Democrats have a stronghold in the state legislature, but her indictment is a political shock wave less than two weeks before the national midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
While federal officials have historically avoided taking public steps in politically fraught cases ahead of elections, the case against Lucas is the second prominent action the administration has taken against a Democratic critic of Trump in the past 10 days.
Last week, federal officers searched the D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, who is up for reelection, as part of an immigration probe. Like Lucas, the congresswoman from Minnesota is a Democrat who has assailed Trump.
Lucas’s daughter, Lisa Lucas Burke, who was also charged Thursday, is on the ballot in November for a Portsmouth City Council seat.
Blanche defended the decision to bring the charges when they did, saying that the investigation into Lucas predated Trump’s election in 2024.
“I think it is my responsibility and Director Patel’s to be open and transparent about charges that we are bringing,” Blanche said. “There has been public reporting on this.”
Virginia decriminalized marijuana possession and legalized medical marijuana sales in 2020. The state also legalized its sale for adult recreational use this year. Permits for nonmedical, recreational sales are set to be issued beginning next year.
Lucas sponsored key legislation to legalize recreational marijuana in the state.
According to the indictment, Lucas and her relatives created a business to sell marijuana for recreational sales in 2021. That business often operated under a fake name to procure marijuana, according to the indictment.
The indictment also alleges that Lucas used her political influence to enact legislation and regulations that would help her cannabis business.
The FBI in May raided Lucas’s Portsmouth offices and a cannabis retail business she co-owns.
At the time, Lucas’s longtime political consultant, Ben Tribbett, said the raided offices were primarily dedicated to the state lawmaker’s various business interests and that no items related to her legislative career were seized.
The indictment unsealed Thursday says that authorities seized large amounts of marijuana from the business.
Lucas and Virginia Democrats have raised questions about the motivation behind the case, noting that the Justice Department under Trump has aggressively targeted his political foes.
Lucas is a character of the rough-hewn port city where she was born. She is the oldest of seven children, and her father drove a forklift at the segregated Norfolk Naval Shipyard. After Lucas dropped out of high school to have her first child, she also took a job at the shipyard, eventually becoming a pipe fitter.
By the time she was 21, Lucas was married and the mother of three children. Her ambition and imperious manner helped her rise in the Democratic power structure of Portsmouth. She became the first African American woman to serve on the city council and was a longtime community activist before winning election to the Virginia Senate in 1991.
Known for her stylish dress and sharp tongue, Lucas eventually became the first Black woman to serve as president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate and is chairwoman of the Finance and Appropriations Committee, giving her significant control over the state’s budget.
She has never been shy about wielding political power. In 2024, Lucas used her authority over the state budget to almost single-handedly block the attempt of then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin (R) to build a major sports arena in Alexandria. She then stood in the background smiling for news cameras as Youngkin angrily denounced her to reporters.
Earlier this year, Lucas defied Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a fellow Democrat, by holding up passage of the state budget until she could get a deal to limit tax benefits to data center developers. Lucas also was a driving force behind the push by Virginia lawmakers to draw new congressional boundaries this year to favor Democrats, again defying Spanberger’s wishes.
Voters approved the referendum to redraw the state’s congressional map, but it was overturned by the state Supreme Court.
Lucas has built a large social media following by criticizing Republicans online. She is also no stranger to controversy. During the 2020 protests against racial injustice and police brutality, Lucas spoke to a crowd gathered around a Confederate statue in Portsmouth. Shortly after she left, a man was gravely injured when protesters pulled down the statue.
The local prosecutor said Lucas had incited the crowd and charged her with a felony. The case was eventually dropped. Lucas’s defense lawyer was Del. Don Scott (D-Portsmouth), who is now the first African American to serve as speaker of the Virginia House of Delegates.
Lucas has extensive business and real estate holdings in Portsmouth and was instrumental in bringing a casino to the city, where her daughter has served on city council.
The indictment makes clear that Lucas did not try to hide that she was running a marijuana business.
The indictment states: “On January 24, 2022, LOUISE LUCAS posted on social media that “I’m a 78 year grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannibis store. And I’m the last thing standing between The GOP and total control of Virginia. That worth an RT!”
Perry Stein covers the Justice Department and FBI for The Washington Post. Greg Schneider covers Virginia from the Richmond bureau.
Jeremy Roebuck and Salvador Rizzo contributed to this report.

sources.text:
The Briefing:
- Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore Louise Lucas, 82, faces five federal felony counts — racketeering conspiracy, marijuana distribution, money laundering, honest services fraud through bribery, and maintaining drug-involved premises — after a grand jury in the Eastern District of Virginia returned an eight-count indictment on October 14.
- Prosecutors allege Lucas, her two daughters, her grandson, and three associates ran the "Lucas Enterprise," a multi-year marijuana network estimated at $4.5 million, with Lucas allegedly using her Senate committee chairmanship to shield the operation from scrutiny and tilt cannabis legislation in its favor.
- Lucas surrendered to federal authorities Thursday morning and is calling the case political intimidation; Democratic allies note the investigation was opened under the Biden administration.
Virginia Senate President Pro Tempore Louise Lucas — 82 years old, more than three decades in office, and among the most consequential Democrats in state government — surrendered to federal authorities Thursday morning after a grand jury charged her alongside six co-defendants in what the U.S. Department of Justice calls the "Lucas Enterprise": an alleged criminal marijuana distribution network anchored in Portsmouth, Virginia, that prosecutors say operated behind the cover of her considerable legislative power.
An Eight-Count Indictment Unsealed in Norfolk
The eight-count federal indictment, approved by a grand jury on October 14 and unsealed at a news conference in Norfolk on Thursday, formally charges Lucas on five felony counts: racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute marijuana, money laundering, honest services fraud through bribery, and maintaining drug-involved premises. Three of the other defendants in the case — Prince Albert William Hudson III, Tamika Johnson, and business associate Carlton Upton Jr. — face a broader version of the charging document that additionally includes wire fraud and firearms-related counts. Lucas herself is not among those charged in connection with the weapons recovered during the investigation.
At Thursday's news conference, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the indictment portrays a public servant who elevated personal financial gain above the constituents she was elected to represent. FBI Director Kash Patel amplified that point, describing the alleged scheme as a five-year operation prosecutors estimate generated roughly $4.5 million — and in which, he said, the senator converted her chairmanship of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee into what amounted to a shield for the criminal enterprise.
Family Members at the Core of the Alleged Operation
The six co-defendants named alongside Lucas include two daughters — Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb — her grandson Ryan Eichelberger, Chesapeake-based business partner Carlton Upton Jr., 54, and the two additional defendants charged with broader offenses. Prosecutors allege Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger handled the acquisition and distribution of marijuana and managed day-to-day operations at The Cannabis Outlet, the Portsmouth cannabis store Lucas co-opened with Lucas-Burke in 2021. Upton ran a sister location called The CBD Shoppe and, the government alleges, worked with Lucas to pursue a recreational marijuana license that would expand the enterprise's footprint.
A Senate Committee Chair Allegedly Turned Into a Shield
The most politically significant allegation in the case is the government's contention that Lucas did not simply operate a cannabis business — she allegedly deployed her position as chairwoman of Virginia's most powerful budget committee to ward off law enforcement and steer the state's emerging cannabis regulatory framework toward the enterprise's financial benefit.
The indictment further alleges that in August 2022, Lucas paid $750,000 to acquire full ownership of a shell company tied to a co-conspirator's expected recreational marijuana license — a financial interest she allegedly did not disclose on the mandatory state ethics filings required of all legislators. Prosecutors say she subsequently met with that co-conspirator at her Capitol complex office, receiving a partial repayment the government characterizes as a bribery arrangement, while also communicating with other officials — including fellow legislators — about that person's prospects for obtaining a marijuana license contingent on that payment.
Two Storefronts, One Corporate Shell, and a Pandemic Loan Allegation
The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe, the two retail operations at the heart of the alleged scheme, both operate under a holding company called VA Freedom Life. That entity was established in 2019 — before Virginia built out a fully regulated recreational cannabis marketplace — and Lucas's partner Upton has been associated with it since its founding. Prosecutors allege that in April 2020, Upton submitted materially false statements on a federal Economic Injury Disaster Loan application on behalf of VA Freedom Life, resulting in the government disbursing $11,800 in pandemic-era relief funds to the company under false pretenses.
Raids in May, Wiretaps by Summer, and a Congressman's Intercepted Calls
Thursday's indictment is the formal culmination of an investigation that had been building publicly for months. On May 6, FBI agents executed court-authorized search warrants simultaneously at Lucas's Portsmouth legislative office, The Cannabis Outlet, and The CBD Shoppe, recovering marijuana and firearms at both retail locations. By September, it had come to light that investigators had obtained judicial authorizations to monitor Lucas's phone — surveillance broad enough to capture calls she held with at least one sitting member of Congress. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA) disclosed publicly that the FBI had intercepted his calls with Lucas during a window spanning March through April — a period he described as politically sensitive given ongoing redistricting battles in Virginia.
Among the communications referenced in the indictment is an intercepted exchange in which Lucas allegedly described the cannabis business as her clearest remaining path to building lasting wealth for her family — a statement prosecutors argue reveals the personal financial motive driving the alleged conspiracy.
Lucas Vows to Fight: "I Will Not Be Intimidated"
Lucas surrendered to federal authorities Thursday morning and moved quickly to reframe the case on political terrain. In a statement posted to X following her surrender, she invoked her experience growing up under Jim Crow and pledged to resist what she characterized as an effort to silence her. "I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied," she wrote. The language echoed what she had said after the May raids, when she described the FBI's actions as reflecting "a clear pattern from this administration" and connected them to Virginia redistricting battles that had made her a central figure in Democratic resistance to Republican electoral strategy.
Lucas has been a member of the Virginia Senate since 1992, when she was sworn into office following her November 1991 election — more than three decades representing the 18th District in southeastern Virginia. In December 2019, following that fall's state elections, she became the first woman and first African American ever chosen as Virginia Senate president pro tempore, a role she has held since January 2020. Throughout her career, she has been a vocal advocate for marijuana decriminalization and criminal justice reform, consistently arguing that drug enforcement has fallen disproportionately on communities of color.
Where Each Party Stands
Democratic colleagues in the chamber urged restraint. Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell noted that the indictment contains allegations, not convictions, and that Lucas is entitled to the presumption of innocence. Several Democrats also pointed to the fact that the federal investigation predates the current administration — having been opened during President Biden's term — a detail that complicates any straightforward reading of the charges as purely partisan in origin. Republican lawmakers drew the opposite conclusion, arguing the case underscores that no length of service or degree of legislative influence can insulate any elected official from federal accountability.
All seven defendants are presumed innocent under the law. Each charge alleged in the indictment must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt before any jury for a conviction to stand.

Virginia state senator, six others indicted in federal cannabis corruption case
State Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, faces federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges tied to a cannabis business she co-owns. Prosecutors allege she used her legislative influence to benefit the business.(Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
State Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democrats, was indicted on federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges, with prosecutors alleging she used her legislative influence to protect and enrich a cannabis business she co-owns.
Lucas, 82, surrendered to authorities, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a news conference in Norfolk Thursday. Six others, including family members and close associates, were also in custody in connection with the alleged scheme.
The eight-count indictment, unsealed Thursday morning, charges Lucas with racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and maintaining drug-involved premises.
The indictment also includes firearms and wire fraud charges against other defendants.
Lucas struck a defiant tone in a statement posted on X following her indictment, accusing federal authorities of trying to silence her.
“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them,” she wrote. “I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now. I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”
The unsealing of the charges against the longtime senator and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump comes 12 days before the midterm elections.
The investigation predates the Trump administration, but the timing is unusual because federal authorities have typically avoided overt investigative steps involving political figures so close to an election.
Lucas is not on the ballot this year but has ties to prominent Democrats who are.
“We’re here today because of facts and evidence, which led to this investigation to begin many years ago, and facts and evidence that led to the grand jury to indict Senator Lucas and her alleged co-conspirators,” Blanche said.
Prosecutors allege Lucas directed an organization they called the “Lucas Enterprise,” arranging the acquisition and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana and supervising the laundering of proceeds.
FBI Director Kash Patel said prosecutors believe Lucas and her associates accumulated nearly $5 million in proceeds from the alleged criminal enterprise over almost five years.
“The purpose of her enterprise included trafficking large quantities of illegal marijuana, creating generational wealth for members and associates of her criminal enterprise,” FBI Director Kash Patel said during the news conference.
Prosecutors also allege Lucas used her position as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the operation from criminal scrutiny and influence legislation benefiting it.
Marijuana is legal to use recreationally in Virginia but not to sell. Earlier this year, lawmakers passed a legislative framework creating a recreational weed marketplace that is set to launch next summer.
Blanche on Thursday accused Lucas of betraying the public’s trust.
“Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself,” he said. “But the charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve.”
    Prosecutors outline business dealings
According to Blanche, Lucas’ associates included her daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and her grandson, Ryan Eichelberger, as well as Carlton Upton Jr, Prince Albert William Hudson III and Tamika Johnson.
Lucas and Lucas-Burke opened The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth in 2021. Prosecutors allege Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger acquired marijuana, supervised its distribution and managed the store for the enterprise.
Upton was Lucas’ business partner in VA Freedom Life, an umbrella for The CBD Shoppe and The Cannabis Outlet beginning in 2019, according to the indictment.
Upton managed The CBD Shoppe and allegedly worked with Lucas to obtain a recreational marijuana license benefiting the enterprise.
Prosecutors also allege Upton made materially false statements on an April 2020 application for an Economic Injury Disaster Loan for Virginia Freedom Life. The loan was funded for $11,800.
Another allegation centers on a $750,000 payment Lucas allegedly made in August 2022 for full ownership of a business serving as a shell holding company for a co-conspirator’s expected Virginia recreational marijuana license.
Prosecutors allege Lucas failed to reveal that interest on required financial disclosure forms. They say she met with the co-conspirator at her Capitol complex office to receive a partial repayment and discussed the person’s qualification for a marijuana license with officials, including legislators, depending on her receipt of a bribery payment.
“Yes, we can make a lot of money but, before we start down that road again; how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me with arrangements for the balance. Then we can talk about future business plans,” she wrote in a text message to the unnamed co-conspirator in November of last year.
Lucas had identified herself as president and CEO of VA Freedom Life on a February 2022 Statement of Economic Interests, according to the release.
Patel said the alleged operation also involved “recycling drug proceeds to expand the operation that she launched and created, and steering marijuana licenses to entities in which members held financial interest.”
The case became public May 6, when federal agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and cannabis businesses. The Justice Department said agents recovered marijuana and firearms at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe.
At the scene, FBI spokeswoman Cassandra Temple told the Mercury: “We are conducting court-authorized law enforcement activity today.” She declined to answer additional questions.
Fox News, which first reported the operation, said staffers were ordered out of Lucas’ office while agents searched. Witnesses saw agents carrying boxes from the building. The network also reported that armed SWAT officers ordered people out of the adjacent Cannabis Outlet and that at least three people were handcuffed.
Lucas arrived after the operation began and told a reporter she did not know what it concerned.
    Lucas has called investigation intimidation
After the May searches, Lucas characterized the federal action as political intimidation, saying it was “about far more than one state senator” and reflected “a clear pattern from this administration.”
In a statement on X at the time, she linked the raid to the redistricting referendum voters approved in April, saying Virginians had voted to “stop Trump’s scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections.” The Supreme Court of Virginia later overturned the referendum.
“I am not backing down, and I will keep fighting for the people of Portsmouth and the commonwealth of Virginia,” she said.
Lucas has served in the Senate since 1992 and as president pro tempore since 2020. Her finance committee chairmanship gives her considerable influence over the state budget, taxes and spending.
Earlier this year, she pushed to end or scale back sales and use tax exemptions for data centers, arguing the incentives had become too costly and strained Virginia’s electric grid and infrastructure. Resistance from House Democrats and Gov. Abigail Spanberger contributed to a monthslong intraparty budget impasse.
What the indictment means for Lucas’ role in the Senate and the upcoming legislative session remained unclear as of Thursday morning.
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, urged restraint in responding to the charges against his Democratic colleague.
“The federal indictment unsealed this week contains serious allegations, and Senator Lucas is entitled to the same presumption of innocence that every American receives,” Surovell said in a statement.
“She is innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. I will not comment on the evidence in this case, and I urge others to show the same restraint.”
Spanberger also emphasized Lucas’ presumption of innocence but criticized the timing of the indictment.
“She and her family deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented,” Spanberger said in a statement Thursday afternoon.
“The timing of this indictment undermines the U.S. Department of Justice’s previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions — to include indictments or significant investigative steps — close to an election and sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice.”
Another top Democrat to defend Lucas’ right to due process while criticizing the Trump administration’s handling of the case was Virginia House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth.
“The Trump administration’s weaponization of the justice system is deeply troubling — as are the allegations made in this indictment,” Scott said in a statement. “Today we have heard only from the Trump administration, and Senator Lucas will have her chance to respond to these charges in court.”
House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Scott, said the allegations against Lucas should be handled by the courts.
“The charges against Senator Lucas are serious, and go beyond the world of politics. They will be resolved via our judicial system, as they should,” Kilgore said in a statement.
Lucas’ cannabis business had drawn scrutiny years before the federal searches. Lucas co-sponsored legislation legalizing simple marijuana possession in 2021, but that change did not establish a regulated recreational retail marketplace.
A 2022 Mercury investigation found labeling discrepancies and quantities of delta-9 THC that made two tested products from The Cannabis Outlet illegal to sell under Virginia law at the time.
One cereal bar contained substantially less total THC than its packaging advertised. The reporting examined broader concerns about unregulated cannabis products following legalization of possession.
In a Feb. 9, 2026, phone call, Lucas allegedly discussed pending recreational marijuana legislation and the possibility of an unnamed co-conspirator obtaining a license and sharing the proceeds with her, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors quote her describing it as “our last chance at generational wealth” and saying, “I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

NORFOLK, Va. -- Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the state's most powerful Democrats, was charged on Thursday in connection with what federal authorities alleged was a role leading a wide-ranging criminal enterprise that acquired and distributed large quantities of marijuana and laundered the proceeds.
Lucas, who has been in elected office for decades, used her political power to insulate the operation from scrutiny, according to an indictment charging her and six other defendants, including several of her relatives. She "put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve," said U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, who spoke at a news conference with FBI Director Kash Patel.
Lucas surrendered, a Justice Department spokesperson said, and was expected to make an initial appearance in federal court on Thursday afternoon.
The charges, including drug trafficking and money laundering, came after the FBI searched Lucas' hometown office and a cannabis shop in which she has a stake in May. At the time of the search, Lucas — who has been a vocal critic of Republican President Donald Trump's administration — characterized it as an attempt to intimidate her.
"This is the circus we always expected it to be, and we will wait for further details to have a more specific response," said Brian Woolfolk, chief counsel for the L. Louise Lucas Legal Defense Fund.
A statement attributed to Lucas posted on her social media account did not directly address the substance of the charges but said Thursday's actions amounted to the federal government wielding its "full weight" against a great-grandmother.
"I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down," Lucas said in the statement.
The brash 82-year-old lawmaker has spent decades ascending the ranks of Virginia politics and has served since 1992 in the state Senate, where she is the president pro tempore, overseeing the chamber in the lieutenant governor's absence. More significantly, she leads the powerful Senate finance committee, through which all legislation with any budget impact must flow. She's used the position to stop and ultimately kill legislation she opposes.
The indictment comes as Trump's Justice Department has faced intense scrutiny over investigations and prosecutions against foes of the president that critics have called politically motivated.
Blanche rejected any suggestion that politics played a role in Lucas' case, noting that the investigation began well before the second Trump administration started in January 2025.
"We don't do political paybacks," Blanche told reporters.
A person familiar with the May search told The Associated Press at the time that the probe was opened during Democratic President Joe Biden's administration.
Patel said in a statement that the charges allege "Lucas and a close-knit group of family members and associates orchestrated a multi-year scheme to enrich their own criminal marijuana enterprise, 'the Lucas Enterprise' — using Lucas' position as Chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influencing legislation to financially benefit themselves."
"No one is above the law," the statement said, "and this FBI will continue to follow the facts with our Justice Department and ensure those responsible for criminal conduct are held accountable."
A forceful advocate of legalizing marijuana, Lucas partnered in opening the shop, The Cannabis Outlet, in 2021, selling hemp and CBD products. Lucas, who represents a district that includes her hometown of coastal Portsmouth, operates with a sometimes-profane, unapologetic style that's drawn comparisons to Trump.

sources.text:
Politics
Top Virginia Senator Faces Federal Marijuana And Fraud Charges
“The purpose of her enterprise included trafficking large quantities of illegal marijuana, creating generational wealth for members and associates of her criminal enterprise.”
By Markus Schmidt, Virginia Mercury
State Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democrats, was indicted on federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges, with prosecutors alleging she used her legislative influence to protect and enrich a cannabis business she co-owns.
Lucas, 82, surrendered to authorities, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a news conference in Norfolk Thursday. Six others, including family members and close associates, were also in custody in connection with the alleged scheme.
The eight-count indictment, unsealed Thursday morning, charges Lucas with racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and maintaining drug-involved premises.
The indictment also includes firearms and wire fraud charges against other defendants.
Lucas struck a defiant tone in a statement posted on X following her indictment, accusing federal authorities of trying to silence her.
“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them,” she wrote. “I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now. I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”
The unsealing of the charges against the longtime senator and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump comes 12 days before the midterm elections.
The investigation predates the Trump administration, but the timing is unusual because federal authorities have typically avoided overt investigative steps involving political figures so close to an election.
Lucas is not on the ballot this year but has ties to prominent Democrats who are.
“We’re here today because of facts and evidence, which led to this investigation to begin many years ago, and facts and evidence that led to the grand jury to indict Senator Lucas and her alleged co-conspirators,” Blanche said.
Prosecutors allege Lucas directed an organization they called the “Lucas Enterprise,” arranging the acquisition and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana and supervising the laundering of proceeds.
FBI Director Kash Patel said prosecutors believe Lucas and her associates accumulated nearly $5 million in proceeds from the alleged criminal enterprise over almost five years.
“The purpose of her enterprise included trafficking large quantities of illegal marijuana, creating generational wealth for members and associates of her criminal enterprise,” FBI Director Kash Patel said during the news conference.
Marijuana is legal to use recreationally in Virginia but not to sell. Earlier this year, lawmakers passed a legislative framework creating a recreational weed marketplace that is set to launch next summer.
Prosecutors also allege Lucas used her position as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the operation from criminal scrutiny and influence legislation benefiting it.
Blanche on Thursday accused Lucas of betraying the public’s trust.
“Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself,” he said. “But the charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve.”
Prosecutors outline business dealings
According to Blanche, Lucas’ associates included her daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and her grandson, Ryan Eichelberger, as well as Carlton Upton Jr, Prince Albert William Hudson III and Tamika Johnson.
Lucas and Lucas-Burke opened The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth in 2021. Prosecutors allege Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger acquired marijuana, supervised its distribution and managed the store for the enterprise.
Upton was Lucas’ business partner in VA Freedom Life, an umbrella for The CBD Shoppe and The Cannabis Outlet beginning in 2019, according to the press release.
Upton managed The CBD Shoppe and allegedly worked with Lucas to obtain a recreational marijuana license benefiting the enterprise.
Prosecutors also allege Upton made materially false statements on an April 2020 application for an Economic Injury Disaster Loan for Virginia Freedom Life. The loan was funded for $11,800.
Another allegation centers on a $750,000 payment Lucas allegedly made in August 2022 for full ownership of a business serving as a shell holding company for a co-conspirator’s expected Virginia recreational marijuana license.
Prosecutors allege Lucas failed to reveal that interest on required financial disclosure forms. They say she met with the co-conspirator at her Capitol complex office to receive a partial repayment and discussed the person’s qualification for a marijuana license with officials, including legislators, depending on her receipt of a bribery payment.
Lucas had identified herself as president and CEO of VA Freedom Life on a February 2022 Statement of Economic Interests, according to the release.
Patel said the alleged operation also involved “recycling drug proceeds to expand the operation that she launched and created, and steering marijuana licenses to entities in which members held financial interest.”
The case became public May 6, when federal agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and cannabis businesses. The Justice Department said agents recovered marijuana and firearms at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe.
At the scene, FBI spokeswoman Cassandra Temple told the Mercury: “We are conducting court-authorized law enforcement activity today.” She declined to answer additional questions.
Fox News, which first reported the operation, said staffers were ordered out of Lucas’ office while agents searched. Witnesses saw agents carrying boxes from the building. The network also reported that armed SWAT officers ordered people out of the adjacent Cannabis Outlet and that at least three people were handcuffed.
Lucas arrived after the operation began and told a reporter she did not know what it concerned.
Lucas has called investigation intimidation
After the May searches, Lucas characterized the federal action as political intimidation, saying it was “about far more than one state senator” and reflected “a clear pattern from this administration.”
In a statement on X at the time, she linked the raid to the redistricting referendum voters approved in April, saying Virginians had voted to “stop Trump’s scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections.” The Supreme Court of Virginia later overturned the referendum.
“I am not backing down, and I will keep fighting for the people of Portsmouth and the commonwealth of Virginia,” she said.
Lucas has served in the Senate since 1992 and as president pro tempore since 2020. Her finance committee chairmanship gives her considerable influence over the state budget, taxes and spending.
Earlier this year, she pushed to end or scale back sales and use tax exemptions for data centers, arguing the incentives had become too costly and strained Virginia’s electric grid and infrastructure. Resistance from House Democrats and Gov. Abigail Spanberger contributed to a monthslong intraparty budget impasse.
What the indictment means for Lucas’ role in the Senate and the upcoming legislative session remained unclear as of Thursday morning.
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, urged restraint in responding to the charges against his Democratic colleague.
“The federal indictment unsealed this week contains serious allegations, and Senator Lucas is entitled to the same presumption of innocence that every American receives,” Surovell said in a statement.
“She is innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. I will not comment on the evidence in this case, and I urge others to show the same restraint.”
Lucas’ cannabis business had drawn scrutiny years before the federal searches. Lucas co-sponsored legislation legalizing simple marijuana possession in 2021, but that change did not establish a regulated recreational retail marketplace.
A 2022 Mercury investigation found labeling discrepancies and quantities of delta-9 THC that made two tested products from The Cannabis Outlet illegal to sell under Virginia law at the time.
One cereal bar contained substantially less total THC than its packaging advertised. The reporting examined broader concerns about unregulated cannabis products following legalization of possession.

 In his explanation of the case, Blanche emphasized the alleged abuse of public trust by an elected official.

Patel, likewise, called the findings evidence of the "epitome of hypocrisy for a public official," adding that the alleged conspiracy resulted in an estimated $5 million in ill-gotten gains.

At the time, Lucas painted the raid as a politically motivated attack, saying, "I am not backing down, and I will keep fighting for the people of Portsmouth and the Commonwealth of Virginia."
The allegations in the indictment stretch back at least to 2019 and extend to the present day. And some of the more recent evidence has caught many observers' attention.
On a recorded call with an unindicted co-conspirator back in February, Lucas allegedly discussed "the possibility of UCC #2 receiving a license and sharing the proceeds with her because 'this is our last chance at generational wealth. ...I've got too old to not be greedy.'"
Days before at the end of January 2026, according to the indictment, Lucas allegedly discussed marijuana and marijuana licensing as a way for her to "get generational wealth and this is my last chance."

Blaze News previously reported that the investigation was initiated by President Joe Biden, citing the AP.

sources.text:
Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas, one of the state’s most influential Democrats, has been indicted on drug-trafficking and money-laundering charges tied to a cannabis business operated by her family.
Lucas, 82, was charged Thursday with racketeering and conspiracy to commit money laundering in connection with a broad public-corruption investigation.
The case focuses on The Cannabis Outlet, a marijuana company owned by Lucas and her relatives. Prosecutors allege the business was used to “disguise the proceeds of illegal marijuana distribution.”
Lucas has long advocated for marijuana legalization, but prosecutors say she also promoted legalization in the Virginia Senate for personal gain. Her indictment cites text messages in which she allegedly discussed making “a lot of money” from the policy.
During a February 2026 phone call, Lucas allegedly told a co-conspirator that she had her “last chance at generational wealth” and had “gotten too old not to be greedy.”
According to the indictment, Lucas allegedly “used her political position” to “insulate” herself and members of her family from prosecution.
The 82-year-old senator reportedly surrendered to authorities Thursday. She was indicted alongside roughly six other alleged co-conspirators, including two of her daughters and a nephew.
At a news conference Thursday, FBI Director Kash Patel said Lucas had amassed nearly $5 million “in ill-gotten gains through her criminal enterprise.”
Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas, 82, was charged Thursday with racketeering and conspiracy to commit money laundering in a sweeping public-corruption investigation
FBI Director Kash Patel and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the charges at a news conference Thursday
Federal agents searched Lucas’s office and The Cannabis Outlet store in Portsmouth, Virginia, in May.
The indictment alleges that members of the conspiracy relied on “various business entities” to conduct “illegal marijuana distribution,” with “wealth accumulation” as their ultimate objective.
In a statement posted to social media Thursday, Lucas vowed to continue fighting. She wrote that the “full weight of the federal government” had been brought against an “82-year-old great-grandmother.”
“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back and I’m not stopping now.
“I’m not new to this. I’m true to this. I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”
The investigation into Lucas began before the Trump administration, according to NBC News.
Lucas has been a prominent voice for marijuana legalization in Virginia and serves as president pro tempore of the state Senate, making her one of the state’s most powerful Democrats.
She also chairs the influential Senate Finance Committee, which handles legislation with budgetary implications. Prosecutors allege Lucas used that position to help expand her family’s cannabis business, including by securing legalization in 2021 and paving the way for statewide retail sales by July 2027.

Although Lucas helped advance legalization legislation, prosecutors allege she also obtained large quantities of marijuana through a co-conspirator from outside Virginia’s five licensed cannabis growers.
Lucas, Virginia’s president pro tempore and one of the state’s most powerful Democrats, allegedly “used her political position” to “insulate” herself and her family from prosecution
Federal agents seen raiding Lucas’s office in Portsmouth, Virginia in May
According to Lucas’s indictment, the Democrat allegedly paid $750,000 to an unindicted co-conspirator in August 2022 for a 100% stake in a shell company called ‘Mama’s Chicken LLC’, which she ‘expected to obtain a Virginia recreational marijuana license.’
When it became apparent that state laws meant licensed marijuana stores wouldn’t open in Virginia until 2027, Lucas then began pressuring the co-conspirator to return the money within months, according to the indictment.
In November 2025, she allegedly texted that same person telling them she would be pushing forward legislation that would ensure licensed pot stores in Virginia.
She allegedly sent in the message: ‘You know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron. Yes, we can make a lot of money but, before we start down that road again; how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me with arrangements for the balance. Then we can talk about future business plans.’
On February 9, 2026, Lucas allegedly called the person to update them on the pending cannabis legislation, telling them: ‘This is our last chance at generational wealth… I’ve got too old to not be greedy.’
On March 9, Lucas also allegedly called another Virginia legislator to ask for a recreational marijuana license, because she ‘got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling in because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.’
Lucas, who is not up for re-election until 2027, was accused by US Attorney General Todd Blanche of using her influence to put her financial interests above her constituents.
Lucas seen with former President Joe Biden and ex-Virginia Governor Terry McAuliffe
‘The Department of Justice intends to prove that Senator Lucas violated the trust of the people of Portsmouth and Chesapeake, Virginia, and of her state senate colleagues,’ Blanche told a press conference.
‘Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself.’
The case comes as the Justice Department has also brought a high-profile investigation against Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar in Minnesota.
The Justice Department typically does not bring political cases within 60 days of elections to avoid allegations of bias, however Blanche dismissed those concerns when speaking to reporters on Thursday.
‘It’s not even a rule, it’s a practice,’ Blanche said, noting that while many of Lucas’s fellow Democrats may be facing incoming re-elections, she is not on the ballot again until next year.
‘The justice manual speaks very clearly about what the Department of Justice can and can’t do, and we cannot bring a charge if our purpose is improper,’ he said, saying he believes this case was correctly brought.

sources.text:
Federal prosecutors accuse Senate powerbroker Louise Lucas of using her office to protect a marijuana operation involving relatives and associates.
One of Virginia’s most powerful Democrats is facing federal racketeering and drug charges after prosecutors accused her of helping run a family marijuana enterprise — and using her political influence to protect it.
State Sen. L. Louise Lucas, 82, surrendered to authorities Thursday as federal officials unveiled a case involving seven defendants, according to NBC News. The indictment follows a federal investigation that burst into public view when agents searched her Portsmouth office and a cannabis business she co-owns in May.
Prosecutors allege Lucas helped oversee the acquisition and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana — roughly 220 pounds — and the laundering of proceeds, according to the Justice Department statement reported by Fox News.
Authorities describe the alleged operation as the “Lucas Enterprise,” involving a close circle of relatives and associates, including her two daughters and a grandson.
Five Charges Against The Senator
Lucas faces five of the eight counts in the indictment, WJLA reported.
According to WTVR’s review of charging documents, those charges are racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess marijuana with intent to distribute, conspiracy to launder money, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, and maintaining a drug-involved premises.
The allegations reach directly into Lucas’ position as chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee.
FBI Director Kash Patel accused the group of using her authority “to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny” while influencing legislation for its own financial benefit, according to the DOJ statement carried by Fox News.
“Louise Lucas has served in a position of public trust in the Commonwealth of Virginia for over three decades,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in that statement.
“The charges alleged in this indictment reveal the behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” Blanche added.
Wiretap Allegations Add To The Case
NBC News reported that the indictment accuses participants of using business entities to conceal proceeds from illegal marijuana distribution.
The network also reported that prosecutors cited an intercepted February 2026 conversation in which Lucas allegedly described the venture as a “last chance at generational wealth.”
That alleged conversation is part of the government’s case; the accusations have not been proven in court.
Lucas, a longtime Portsmouth lawmaker, also serves as president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate. Her leadership positions have made her a major force in Richmond, placing Thursday’s indictment at the center of the state’s political establishment.
Lucas and Democratic allies have previously questioned whether the investigation was politically motivated, The Washington Post reported. NBC News reported that the investigation began before the current Trump administration.

sources.news_title: Top Democratic Virginia lawmaker charged by DOJ with running illegal cannabis operation
sources.text:
By Andrew Goudsward
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 (Reuters) – A senior Democratic state lawmaker in Virginia was charged with racketeering conspiracy, money laundering and other offenses for allegedly running an illegal cannabis business with members of her family, according to an indictment made public on Thursday.
Virginia State Senator L. Louise Lucas, 82, a long-serving Democrat, was charged along with two of her daughters, her grandson and three others, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors allege that Lucas and her associates arranged for the distribution and sale of large amounts of marijuana. Recreational cannabis dispensaries are not yet legally authorized in the state.
The indictment of a senior Democratic lawmaker comes less than two weeks before the November midterm elections, which will determine control of the US Congress, though Lucas and other members of the Virginia state Senate are not up for reelection this year.
The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has repeatedly investigated and, in some cases, prosecuted prominent critics of the Republican president, and the department faced criticism for raiding Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar’s home last week.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the investigation into Lucas has been ongoing for several years, rejecting suggestions that it was politically motivated.
“The charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” Blanche said during a press conference.
In a statement posted to social media, Lucas did not address the allegations in the indictment, but said the case resulted from her standing up to “people in power.”
“I will not intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down,” Lucas wrote.
Lucas surrendered to authorities on Thursday morning and was due to make her first court appearance later in the day in Norfolk, Virginia, federal court.
Lucas serves as president pro tempore of the state Senate, meaning she leads the legislative body when the lieutenant governor is not present.
She played a leading role in Virginia’s unsuccessful attempt to redraw its legislative districts last year in a bid to keep pace with Republicans who were leading similar efforts in other states.
(Reporting by Andrew Goudsward; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Bill Berkrot)

sources.news_title: ‘I’m not new to this. I’m true to this’: Virginia Sen. L. Louise Lucas fires back after Trump DOJ indictment
sources.text:
The Trump Justice Department has indicted Virginia State Senator L. Louise Lucas, a stalwart Democrat in Virginia politics and frequent critic of President Donald Trump.
According to multiple reports from news outlets, Lucas, 82, and members of her family were charged as part of a long-running corruption investigation into her family’s marijuana business.
The Washington Post reports that the indictment was returned by a federal grand jury last week and unsealed Thursday morning. The indictment accuses Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia State Senate, and her relatives of setting up a business to sell marijuana before the substance was legalized for recreational sales in the state. Lucas reportedly turned herself in to authorities early Thursday while members of her family were arrested.
The indictment of Senator Lucas comes days after the Justice Department raided the Washington, D.C., home of U.S. Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, marking two high-profile law enforcement actions taken against prominent Black female Democrats who have been critical of President Trump just days ahead of Election Day.
According to the indictment, Lucas and her relatives are accused of creating a business to sell marijuana for recreational sales in 2021. It claims the business often operated under a fake name to procure marijuana. The Trump DOJ also alleges that Lucas used her political influence to enact legislation and regulations that would help her cannabis business.
In a statement after the indictment, Lucas said, “Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother.”
“I grew up in Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them,” said Senator Lucas. “I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now.”
The Democrat added, “I’m not new to this. I’m true to this. I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”
Lucas was first elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and made history in 2020 as the first Black woman to serve as Senate president pro tempore. The Virginia Democrat has wielded much power in state politics as a member of the party’s leadership, including as chairwoman of the Finance and Appropriations Committee, which gives her significant control over the state’s budget.
The scrutiny of Lucas’ family-run business first came to light in May, after FBI agents raided her office in Portsmouth, Virginia. At the time, Lucas slammed the federal probe as a politically motivated attempt to intimidate her after she led Virginia Democrats in redistricting the state’s congressional map to benefit their party and push back against a Trump-led effort for Republicans to redraw maps across the country to help the GOP maintain control of Congress in 2027. However, the Virginia Supreme Court struck down the Democratic-led ballot measure approved by Virginia voters.
Senator Lucas dismissed the May FBI raid as a “pattern” from the Trump administration to “intimidate and silence the voices who stand up to them.”
“Virginians sent a powerful message when they voted to stop Trump’s scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections,” Lucas said at the time. “I was proud to help lead that effort and I have never been afraid to stand up to Donald Trump or anyone else that has tried to undermine our democracy. I am not backing down, and I will keep fighting for the people of Portsmouth and the Commonwealth of Virginia.”

sources.news_title: Prosecutors: Lucas' scheme sought ‘generational wealth’
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – State Sen. Louise Lucas and three relatives are among seven defendants charged in a Virginia operation federal prosecutors say involves marijuana and money laundering in an effort to build family wealth.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday in Norfolk that all seven defendants were in federal custody after being arrested or surrendering. They include the 82-year-old Lucas, her daughters Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and her grandson Ryan Eichelberger.
Blanche said his understanding was that Lucas surrendered Thursday morning. She was to appear before a magistrate later in the day. A federal grand jury returned the eight-count indictment Oct. 14.
The indictment describes a Feb. 9, 2026, phone call in which prosecutors say Lucas discussed pending marijuana legislation and the possibility of an associate receiving a license and sharing proceeds with her.
“This is our last chance at generational wealth,” Lucas said, according to the indictment. “I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”
FBI Director Kash Patel described an estimated $4.5 million scheme spanning five years in the Justice Department’s written release. At the news conference, he said its purposes included creating generational wealth, expanding the operation with drug proceeds and steering marijuana licenses toward entities in which members had financial interests.
On social media, Lucas wrote, "Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother. I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now."
Lucas won election to the state Senate in November 1991 and has remained for 34 years. She's been president pro tempore the last six.
Prosecutors say Lucas directed what they call the “Lucas Enterprise,” arranged marijuana purchases and distribution, supervised money laundering and used her political influence to demand and accept a bribe.
According to the Justice Department, Lucas paid $750,000 in August 2022 for full ownership of a shell company tied to an associate’s expected recreational marijuana license. Prosecutors say she failed to disclose the interest, received a partial repayment at her Capitol complex office and discussed the associate’s license qualifications with officials depending on receiving a bribery payment.
Lucas, a Portsmouth Democrat not on the ballot this fall, faces five counts involving racketeering conspiracy, marijuana distribution conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy, honest services fraud conspiracy and maintaining a drug-involved premises.
Other defendants face additional firearms and wire fraud charges. Lucas is not charged with those offenses.
“The charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” Blanche said.
Lucas has served in the Senate since 1992 and as president pro tempore since 2020. She chairs the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee.
In a statement released Thursday, Lucas said, “I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”
Lucas did not respond directly to The Center Square’s request for comment before publication.
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell called the allegations serious and urged restraint, saying Lucas is entitled to the presumption of innocence.
Asked about accusations of political payback, Blanche said the investigation began before President Donald Trump’s reelection.
The case follows the FBI’s May 6 searches in Portsmouth, previously reported by The Center Square. DOJ said agents recovered marijuana and firearms at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe.
All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

State Sen. L. Louise Lucas, 82, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump, faces federal charges of racketeering, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to distribute marijuana, according to the Justice Department.
The arrest marks a stunning development for the veteran Democratic lawmaker, who has spent decades climbing Virginia’s political ranks.
Lucas was among seven people taken into custody in connection with the alleged operation, which federal prosecutors claim involved a cannabis business she co-owns.
According to the indictment, participants “used various business entities” to “disguise the proceeds of illegal marijuana distribution.”
Prosecutors further allege that Lucas “used her political position in the Virginia state senate to insulate” the enterprise “from criminal scrutiny, to further the goal of wealth accumulation.”
The accusations go beyond an ordinary business dispute, raising questions about whether a powerful elected official improperly used her government position to protect a private financial operation.
