sources.news_title: Virginia Sen. L. Louise Lucas indicted, accused of leading a marijuana distribution enterprise
Va. Sen. Louise Lucas, six others indicted in federal cannabis corruption case
sources.text:
Va. Sen. Louise Lucas, six others indicted in federal cannabis corruption case
Prosecutors allege the powerful Portsmouth Democrat used her office to benefit a marijuana enterprise; Lucas says she “won’t be intimidated.’
State Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, faces federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges tied to a cannabis business she co-owns. Prosecutors allege she used her legislative influence to benefit the business.(Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
State Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democrats, was indicted on federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges, with prosecutors alleging she used her legislative influence to protect and enrich a cannabis business she co-owns.
Lucas, 82, surrendered to authorities, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a news conference in Norfolk Thursday. Six others, including family members and close associates, were also in custody in connection with the alleged scheme.
The eight-count indictment, unsealed Thursday morning, charges Lucas with racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and maintaining drug-involved premises.
The indictment also includes firearms and wire fraud charges against other defendants.
Lucas struck a defiant tone in a statement posted on X following her indictment, accusing federal authorities of trying to silence her.
“I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them,” she wrote. “I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now. I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down.”
The unsealing of the charges against the longtime senator and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump comes 12 days before the midterm elections.
The investigation predates the Trump administration, but the timing is unusual because federal authorities have typically avoided overt investigative steps involving political figures so close to an election.
Lucas is not on the ballot this year but has ties to prominent Democrats who are.
“We’re here today because of facts and evidence, which led to this investigation to begin many years ago, and facts and evidence that led to the grand jury to indict Senator Lucas and her alleged co-conspirators,” Blanche said.
Prosecutors allege Lucas directed an organization they called the “Lucas Enterprise,” arranging the acquisition and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana and supervising the laundering of proceeds.
FBI Director Kash Patel said prosecutors believe Lucas and her associates accumulated nearly $5 million in proceeds from the alleged criminal enterprise over almost five years.
“The purpose of her enterprise included trafficking large quantities of illegal marijuana, creating generational wealth for members and associates of her criminal enterprise,” FBI Director Kash Patel said during the news conference.
Prosecutors also allege Lucas used her position as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the operation from criminal scrutiny and influence legislation benefiting it.
Marijuana is legal to use recreationally in Virginia but not to sell. Earlier this year, lawmakers passed a legislative framework creating a recreational weed marketplace that is set to launch next summer.
Blanche on Thursday accused Lucas of betraying the public’s trust.
“Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself,” he said. “But the charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve.”
    Prosecutors outline business dealings
According to Blanche, Lucas’ associates included her daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and her grandson, Ryan Eichelberger, as well as Carlton Upton Jr, Prince Albert William Hudson III and Tamika Johnson.
Lucas and Lucas-Burke opened The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth in 2021. Prosecutors allege Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger acquired marijuana, supervised its distribution and managed the store for the enterprise.
Upton was Lucas’ business partner in VA Freedom Life, an umbrella for The CBD Shoppe and The Cannabis Outlet beginning in 2019, according to the indictment.
Upton managed The CBD Shoppe and allegedly worked with Lucas to obtain a recreational marijuana license benefiting the enterprise.
Prosecutors also allege Upton made materially false statements on an April 2020 application for an Economic Injury Disaster Loan for Virginia Freedom Life. The loan was funded for $11,800.
Another allegation centers on a $750,000 payment Lucas allegedly made in August 2022 for full ownership of a business serving as a shell holding company for a co-conspirator’s expected Virginia recreational marijuana license.
Prosecutors allege Lucas failed to reveal that interest on required financial disclosure forms. They say she met with the co-conspirator at her Capitol complex office to receive a partial repayment and discussed the person’s qualification for a marijuana license with officials, including legislators, depending on her receipt of a bribery payment.
“Yes, we can make a lot of money but, before we start down that road again; how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me with arrangements for the balance. Then we can talk about future business plans,” she wrote in a text message to the unnamed co-conspirator in November of last year.
Lucas had identified herself as president and CEO of VA Freedom Life on a February 2022 Statement of Economic Interests, according to the release.
Patel said the alleged operation also involved “recycling drug proceeds to expand the operation that she launched and created, and steering marijuana licenses to entities in which members held financial interest.”
The case became public May 6, when federal agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and cannabis businesses. The Justice Department said agents recovered marijuana and firearms at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe.
At the scene, FBI spokeswoman Cassandra Temple told the Mercury: “We are conducting court-authorized law enforcement activity today.” She declined to answer additional questions.
Fox News, which first reported the operation, said staffers were ordered out of Lucas’ office while agents searched. Witnesses saw agents carrying boxes from the building. The network also reported that armed SWAT officers ordered people out of the adjacent Cannabis Outlet and that at least three people were handcuffed.
Lucas arrived after the operation began and told a reporter she did not know what it concerned.
    Lucas has called investigation intimidation
After the May searches, Lucas characterized the federal action as political intimidation, saying it was “about far more than one state senator” and reflected “a clear pattern from this administration.”
In a statement on X at the time, she linked the raid to the redistricting referendum voters approved in April, saying Virginians had voted to “stop Trump’s scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections.” The Supreme Court of Virginia later overturned the referendum.
“I am not backing down, and I will keep fighting for the people of Portsmouth and the commonwealth of Virginia,” she said.
Lucas has served in the Senate since 1992 and as president pro tempore since 2020. Her finance committee chairmanship gives her considerable influence over the state budget, taxes and spending.
Earlier this year, she pushed to end or scale back sales and use tax exemptions for data centers, arguing the incentives had become too costly and strained Virginia’s electric grid and infrastructure. Resistance from House Democrats and Gov. Abigail Spanberger contributed to a monthslong intraparty budget impasse.
What the indictment means for Lucas’ role in the Senate and the upcoming legislative session remained unclear as of Thursday morning.
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, urged restraint in responding to the charges against his Democratic colleague.
“The federal indictment unsealed this week contains serious allegations, and Senator Lucas is entitled to the same presumption of innocence that every American receives,” Surovell said in a statement.
“She is innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. I will not comment on the evidence in this case, and I urge others to show the same restraint.”
Spanberger also emphasized Lucas’ presumption of innocence but criticized the timing of the indictment.
“She and her family deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented,” Spanberger said in a statement Thursday afternoon.
“The timing of this indictment undermines the U.S. Department of Justice’s previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions — to include indictments or significant investigative steps — close to an election and sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice.”
Another top Democrat to defend Lucas’ right to due process while criticizing the Trump administration’s handling of the case was Virginia House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth.
“The Trump administration’s weaponization of the justice system is deeply troubling — as are the allegations made in this indictment,” Scott said in a statement. “Today we have heard only from the Trump administration, and Senator Lucas will have her chance to respond to these charges in court.”
House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Scott, said the allegations against Lucas should be handled by the courts.
“The charges against Senator Lucas are serious, and go beyond the world of politics. They will be resolved via our judicial system, as they should,” Kilgore said in a statement.
Lucas’ cannabis business had drawn scrutiny years before the federal searches. Lucas co-sponsored legislation legalizing simple marijuana possession in 2021, but that change did not establish a regulated recreational retail marketplace.
A 2022 Mercury investigation found labeling discrepancies and quantities of delta-9 THC that made two tested products from The Cannabis Outlet illegal to sell under Virginia law at the time.
One cereal bar contained substantially less total THC than its packaging advertised. The reporting examined broader concerns about unregulated cannabis products following legalization of possession.
In a Feb. 9, 2026, phone call, Lucas allegedly discussed pending recreational marijuana legislation and the possibility of an unnamed co-conspirator obtaining a license and sharing the proceeds with her, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors quote her describing it as “our last chance at generational wealth” and saying, “I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

sources.news_title: Virginia State Sen. Lucas Charged With Drug Trafficking, Money Laundering
sources.text:
Federal prosecutors unsealed charges against Democratic Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, the chamber’s president pro tempore, on Oct. 22 for allegedly helping lead a criminal drug trafficking and money laundering operation.
A 45-page indictment that was filed in the Eastern District of Virginia charged Lucas and six others with racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to launder money, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, and maintaining a drug-involved premises.
The powerful Democratic senator approved and directed criminal activities to benefit her Lucas Enterprise, Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news conference announcing the charges, noting that she also allegedly supervised the laundering of proceeds from marijuana sales.
He also said that Lucas is alleged to have “used her political influence to demand and accept a bribe and attempted to influence Virginia legislation for the benefit of herself and her family.”
Also in the news conference, Blanche said that Lucas and the six other co-defendants were “arrested or surrendered for allegedly participating in a large-scale RICO drug trafficking and money laundering conspiracy,” adding that they are currently in federal custody.
Following the announcement of the charges, Lucas wrote in a post on X that she believes that the charges are political in nature and suggested that racial animus also played a role.
“I grew up under Jim Crow,” she wrote, referring to a collection of local and state laws that enforced racial segregation and ended in the mid-20th century. “I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them.”
While Lucas did not elaborate on how the charges relate to segregation, she wrote that she “will not be intimidated” and “will not back down.”
The charges were filed after the FBI in May searched Lucas’s hometown office and a cannabis shop in which she has a stake, she confirmed at the time. At the time of the search, Lucas, who is a critic of President Donald Trump, characterized it as an attempt to intimidate her.
A spokesman for Lucas, Brian Woolfolk, chief counsel for the L. Louise Lucas Legal Defense Fund, told media outlets on Oct. 22 that the charges are “the circus we always expected it to be, and we will wait for further details to have a more specific response.”
The 82-year-old Democratic lawmaker has spent decades rising through Virginia politics and has served in the state Senate since 1992, where she is president pro tempore, overseeing the chamber in the lieutenant governor’s absence.
She also leads the powerful state Senate finance committee, through which all legislation with any budget impact must flow.
An advocate of legalizing marijuana, Lucas partnered in opening the shop, The Cannabis Outlet, in 2021, selling hemp and cannabidiol (CBD) products, according to local media reports.
“Let’s talk about pot,” she wrote in a social media post on X in 2022. “Yes, we legalized it and I even opened the Cannabis Outlet after we did! But the job isn’t done. People are still in jail for something that is legal today.”
Earlier this year, Lucas sponsored a bill, SB62, that would create a process in which incarcerated individuals or those on community supervision for some felony offenses, including marijuana-related offenses, could get an automatic hearing to consider whether the sentences should be modified.
While marijuana is legal to possess in Virginia, recreational retail sales of the drug are not yet underway, though shops across the state do sell other cannabis-derived products.
Lucas also runs a network of companies that provide residential, transportation, and other services to adults with intellectual disabilities, her biography on a state government website states.
FBI Director Kash Patel told reporters in a news conference on the morning of Oct. 22 that the senator is “truly the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official.”
“During her time as Virginia State Senator, instead of enforcing the law, she was actually breaking the law as alleged in the indictment, and then using her position of power and public trust to defend and deflect against her own criminal enterprise,” Patel said.
Woolfolk’s office and the FBI did not immediately respond to an Epoch Times request for comment on Oct. 22.

Lucas allegedly failed to report the interest obtained in this entity on her required Statement of Economic Interests forms. Lucas allegedly met with the co-conspirator at her office at the capitol complex to receive a partial repayment and spoke with other officials, including legislators, about the co-conspirator’s qualification for a recreational marijuana license depending on her receipt of a bribery payment from the co-conspirator.

sources.news_title: Virginia Sen. Louise Lucas indicted; led criminal drug enterprise, feds say
sources.text:
NORFOLK — The Justice Department on Thursday announced a federal grand jury indictment of Virginia Sen. Louise Lucas on felony charges related to suspected marijuana drug trafficking and money laundering.
Prosecutors accused Lucas and six others, including her two daughters, of selling marijuana illegally from Lucas’ licensed CBD shop and conspiring to rig the state’s marijuana licensure process so they would financially benefit.
The announcement comes less than two weeks before midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Lucas’ seat is not on the ballot, but the 82-year-old is a powerful Democrat who has served in the Virginia Senate for 30 years and chairs the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee. She was also a vocal proponent of a failed redistricting effort that would have heavily favored Democrats in Virginia.
Lucas’ legal troubles surfaced in the public sphere in May when FBI agents raided her downtown Portsmouth office, Lucas Lodge LLC, which houses Lucas’ political headquarters and her family business serving adults with intellectual disabilities. They also raided her nearby CBD shop, The Cannabis Outlet.
Justice Department announces charges
According to the indictment unsealed Thursday, Lucas and a close-knit group of associates, including her family members, orchestrated a criminal enterprise with Lucas’ cannabis business. Prosecutors said she approved and directed activities for the enterprise, including arranging for the acquisition and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana and supervising the laundering of marijuana proceeds.
“During her time as Virginia State Senator, instead of enforcing the law, she was actually breaking the law as alleged in the indictment, and then using her position of power and public trust to deflect and defend against her own criminal enterprise,” FBI Director Kash Patel said. “Truly, the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official.”
Patel and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche traveled to Norfolk to announce the charges.
“Through her elected office, Senator Lucas has been a public servant,” Blanche said. “Her first duty should have been looking out for her constituents before herself. But the charges listed in the indictment reflect the alleged behavior of a public servant who put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve.”
“Whether you are a Democrat or a Republican, an elected official, or an everyday citizen, nobody is above the law,” he said.
Patel said at the news conference that Lucas has accumulated “nearly $5 million in ill-gotten gains through her criminal enterprise” over the past five years. “Instead of serving the public as was her job,” Patel said, Lucas “created a criminal enterprise” to illicitly enrich herself through the marijuana business.
The indictment also charges six others, including Lucas’ daughters Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb and grandson Ryan Eichelberger. It also charges Carlton Upton Jr., a former business partner of Lucas’, along with Prince Albert William Hudson III and Tameka Johnson. Lucas-Burke is running for one of three at-large seats on the Portsmouth City Council, and she’s also executive director of Lucas Lodge LLC.
Response from Lucas
Lucas has been in office since 1992. She’s made no secret of her status as a “grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannabis store,” and she’s been known to sample her own supply.
Since the raid, Lucas has repeatedly said she didn’t know what was being investigated.
Lucas turned herself in early Thursday. She appeared in Norfolk’s federal courthouse Thursday afternoon to face her charges. She and five of the six other codefendants were escorted into the courtroom by U.S. Marshals. Lucas was the only one not shackled at the wrists, but she moved slowly with shackles around her ankles.
Each of those charged acknowledged their charges and were released by U.S. Magistrate Judge Robert Krask. Upton turned himself into federal authorities in Georgia and was not present in the Norfolk courtroom.
Neither Lucas nor her attorney addressed the news media outside the courthouse. But Lucas, who is known for a fiery and at times profane social media presence, did not hold back on social media. In a post made ahead of her court appearance, Lucas said she would not be intimidated or bullied and implied the charges were retaliatory by President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice for Lucas’ role as a Democrat in Virginia politics.
“Today, the FBI, the Department of Justice, and the full weight of the federal government have been wielded against an 82-year-old great-grandmother,” she wrote. “I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now.”
Lucas has previously said the products at the Cannabis Outlet are CBD, which is legal in Virginia, rather than THC, which is currently illegal to buy and sell. Virginia is gearing up for a legal retail market set to take effect July of next year.
The indictment
Lucas and Lucas-Burke are both charged with racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to money launder, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, and maintaining a drug-involved premises.
The indictment states that law enforcement made five controlled purchases of marijuana from the Cannabis Outlet between October 2024 and October 2025, and another purchase in July 2026 of two products that “tested positive for marijuana.”
Federal prosecutors contend that in August 2022, Lucas paid $750,000 for a 100% stake in Mama’s Chicken LLC, described in the indictment as a Delaware-based shell company that she and an unnamed co-conspirator were expected to use for a future Virginia recreational marijuana license. Lucas is accused of failing to report this stake on her required Statement of Economic Interests form, required of all state lawmakers.
The indictment alleges the agreement stipulated that the co-conspirator would refund Lucas $525,000 if he hadn’t obtained a license by Dec. 31, 2025. But by October 2022, Lucas began pressing the co-conspirator to return the $750,000.
In November 2025, Lucas allegedly sent the co-conspirator a text message asking for a “good faith payment of the money you owe me” and “then we can talk about future business plans.”
In January, the indictment says the two met at Lucas’ legislative office at the Capitol complex in Richmond, where Lucas received a “partial repayment” totaling $100,000 from the co-conspirator — an amount provided to the co-conspirator by the FBI — in exchange for her continued work to “direct a license” to the co-conspirator.
At that meeting, Lucas allegedly called the president of the Virginia Cannabis Association and the vice chair of the Virginia Beach Cannabis Task Force to inform them she and the co-conspirator were “back in the same tent again.”
Lucas and the co-conspirator allegedly met at her business office in Portsmouth again in January, and she asked for “samples” of marijuana flowers she could try during the scheduled meeting. During the meeting in Portsmouth, the indictment alleges Lucas called Lucas-Burke and Eichelberger to discuss their sources of marijuana supply. When the co-conspirator asked whether The Cannabis Outlet was receiving hemp, Lucas-Burke and Eichelberger both allegedly said “it’s not hemp, it’s THC.”
Following that conversation, Lucas allegedly continued discussing with the co-conspirator that marijuana licensing was a way to “get generational wealth and this is my last chance.”
The same day federal authorities raided Lucas’ businesses in downtown Portsmouth, they also raided Upton’s CBD Shoppe in downtown Norfolk. Upton, the shop’s owner, is suspected of being Lucas’ business partner in the enterprise.
Upton was indicted on three counts of wire fraud in May related to obtaining pandemic era business relief funds. The indictment accuses Lucas of using her political position to obtain a recreational marijuana license” for Upton with the understanding they would split the proceeds. It’s unclear what that is in reference to as Virginia has not yet begun to approve recreational marijuana licenses. Blanche on Thursday was unable to elaborate on the allegation, saying the indictment shows statements made by Lucas and co-conspirators regarding such pursuits were “inconsistent” with the law.
Lucas has maintained that she and Upton severed professional ties in 2022.
“Two or three months in, I saw how messy he was,” Lucas told The Virginian-Pilot in an interview in August. “I said, ‘I’m not going to work with this boy.’ So I went to my lawyer and severed the relationship.”
However, the indictment states that as recently as March 2026, Upton had a meeting with Lucas and called her to tell her, “I only got five licenses, but you know what I mean, you first, so I need to talk to you like before I make any decisions that affect you.”
The FBI was monitoring Lucas’ phone communications in the months leading up to the raid.
The lead federal prosecutor on the case, Eric Hurt, was seen approaching Upton’s attorney at the courthouse Thursday and could be heard asking that his client consider a plea deal.
The aftermath
Virginia Democrats initially speculated the May raid was political retaliation for Lucas’ redistricting campaign. At one point, Lucas sold shirts reading “Ten F****n’ One,” a reference to the proposed maps and a staunch rejection of other, less overtly partisan maps favored by others in her party.
But Democratic lawmakers were fairly measured in their responses to her indictment Thursday, raising questions about Trump’s politicization of the Justice Department, but not inherently jumping to her defense. Following the raid, supporters launched a legal defense fund. Lucas transferred $300,000 in campaign funds to both the legal defense fund and to her law firm — payments made the day before a new state law prohibiting personal use of campaign funds went into effect.
On Thursday, Lucas and her daughter, Lucas-Burke, clutched the hands of family before walking toward the exit of the federal courthouse.
“Smile and wave,” said a pastor who attended court in her support. A wall of press awaited the mother and daughter outside. “She’s very tired,” Lucas’ lawyer said, and ready to return home to rest. “We will live to fight another day.”
Lucas pushed silently through the crowd with her pink sunglasses on toward a Black Ford truck. Portsmouth Sheriff Michael Moore was in the driver’s seat. Lucas stepped inside and the truck pulled away.
Staff writer Peter Dujardin contributed to this report.
